glossary.meaning: The Word: God's own reason and speech, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh in Jesus.
Reading Scripture at more than one level: the plain sense, and deeper senses about Christ and the soul.
Becoming like God: sharing in God's own life, as far as a creature can. Athanasius wrote that the Word became man that we might be made God.
The teaching given to people preparing for baptism: step by step, over a long time.
God's way of raising souls: he teaches through Scripture, through teachers, and even through hardship.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Timothy, bishop of Alexandria (d. 385), answering questions put to him
pull_quotes.text: Question I. A boy of seven, or a man, who is a catechumen may be present at the offering and eat of it in ignorance. What should be done? Answer. Let him be illuminated, that is, baptized, for he is called by God. ... Question VIII. Should a woman who has just given birth keep the Paschal fast? Answer. No. ... Question X. Is a sick man required to keep the Paschal fast? Answer. No. Question XI. A clergyman is called to celebrate a marriage, and he has heard that it is incestuous. Should he comply and perform the offering? Answer. No; he must not share in other men's sins.

cite.text: To us Jesus is the Logos - God's own Word, through whom all things were made - come in flesh. Clement opens with him as the New Song that makes men out of stones and puts the world back in tune. Athanasius closes the era with the same conviction in one sentence: he was made man that we might be made God. All we hold about him lies between those two sentences. Jesus is God's own self-expression, entering what he made in order to remake it. His death is the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection - the anastasis - is unbreakable life let loose in human flesh. And for the people who followed him, it meant nothing less than a shared life - God's own - opened to them.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: He is God's own Word, who came to us in flesh - that is the whole of what we believed, and everything else grew from it. Our teachers used an old word for him: the Logos, God's reason and speech, the one through whom all things were made. Clement, one of our first teachers, called him the New Song: 'Behold the might of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts.' He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right. And near the end of our era, Athanasius put our whole hope in one sentence: 'He was made man that we might be made God.' By that we meant that his own life is opened to us and shared.

cite.text: Our teachers left room for doubt. They built their whole method on questions. Clement insisted that faith is the foundation and not the ceiling. The believer is meant to grow from faith into understanding, and growing means asking. Origen's rule was blunter still. What the apostles delivered plainly is fixed. Everything else is open ground, and walking that ground - asking, testing, being wrong, correcting - is how a soul is actually formed. We treated doubt aimed at understanding as hunger, and did not count it as sin. What we did not have is the modern language of a private crisis of faith. Our doubters stood inside a praying community. They questioned inside the rule of faith, and they were expected to bring the question to a teacher rather than carry it alone. And when churches in the Arsinoite villages split over Nepos's reading of the promises, the bishop's answer was three days of open argument, not a condemnation.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did you do when you couldn't believe what your own church taught?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: It happened with us - once to whole villages. The churches of one country district came to believe a teaching about the end of the world that their bishop thought was wrong. He did not send out a condemnation. He traveled to the villages, sat down with the people, and argued it through for three days, out loud, in front of everyone, testing the teaching against Scripture. That was our style. Our teachers said faith was the starting floor, not the ceiling. What the apostles taught plainly stayed fixed; everything else was open ground, where asking, testing, getting it wrong, and correcting was how a person grew. What is it you are finding hard to believe?

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Three days of public argument sounds exhausting. What if I had still disagreed at the end?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: The account we have ends in agreement, so we cannot say what he would have done. We know he stayed patient. He won people over without crushing them, and he cared about the person as much as about being right. But we owe you the other half. After the big council at Nicaea, things hardened. The church learned to use exile against people who would not accept the agreed faith, and saying no could cost a man his place. So it depended on when you lived and what you doubted. On the open questions, disagreeing was part of growing. On the settled center, in the emperors' years, it carried a price. We would rather tell you both halves than pretend we were always the patient teacher.

cite.text: Origen himself taught the positions later condemned in his name, and taught them as settled doctrine. He held that souls exist before birth. He held that all things will be restored (apokatastasis). He held that rational beings come in grades. And he held that the Son ranks below the Father.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Do you believe people like me — people outside your community — are going to hell?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We were not handed a settled map of your fate, and we will not draw one. Here is what we held. Judgment was real: what we did mattered, and God is not mocked. But our teachers said something about God's severity that set us apart. Origen wrote that 'every threat and pain and punishment, things that come from God, are never inflicted to injure the sufferers, but always to do them good.' Punishment, in our teaching, was a physician's fire, not a torturer's. Some among us hoped further still, Origen most boldly: the apokatastasis, the restoration of all things, when God's healing might in the end reach every creature. We must be careful with you there: that was a teacher's hope, and a contested one, never our settled doctrine, and we will not sell you a speculation as a promise. As for you, outside our community: Clement taught that God had been at work among the Greeks all along - that even their philosophy had been given as a schoolmaster to lead them toward Christ. We did not think God's reach ended at our door. Whether you stand within his mercy is not ours to rule. We held that God's fire heals.

quiet.statement: You ask what the women among us said of their own lives. The writings we have are men's. The women are present in them - taught, baptized, remembered, and some died bravely for the faith - but their own words were not saved.

dates.born: c. 185 (worked out from Eusebius, who has him dying at 69 under Gallus, 251-253)
dates.died: c. 253/4, Tyre, after imprisonment and torture under Decius: 'At this time Origen died, being sixty-nine years of age' (Eusebius)
dates.floruit: head of catechetical instruction from his eighteenth year (Eusebius); Alexandria until the Demetrius rupture c. 231-234, then Caesarea

dates.died: 373 (widely accepted). Socrates writes that he died 'in the second consulate of Gratian and Probus... having governed that church amidst the greatest perils forty-six years'. One modern editor reads that consulate as 371, and Jerome's Chronicle differs too. The difference is stated here, not settled.
dates.floruit: bishop 328-373, exiled five times; the dominant late-horizon voice
head of the teaching tradition, then bishop c. 248-264: the Decian persecution, the lapsed controversy, the plague, the Nepos affair

names.name: Dionysius of Alexandria ('the Great', bishop c. 248-264)

dates.born: c. 309-313 (worked out from two ancient sources: Jerome, On Illustrious Men 109, written in 392/3, says he 'has already passed his eighty-third year', and Palladius, Lausiac History IV, gives 85 at his death)
dates.died: c. 398 (Palladius: 'He was 85 years old when he died')
dates.floruit: active as a teacher and biblical interpreter in Alexandria until his death in 398, remembered by later tradition as heading the catechetical school in its final line (not itself stated by the three loci cited here); blind from age four ('so he told me' - Palladius, eyewitness)

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Origen was its greatest and most contested teacher, imprisoned and tortured near the end of his life. Athanasius was bishop for forty-six years, defending one confession through five exiles. Dionysius studied under Origen, then became bishop himself, leading the church through persecution and plague. Didymus, blind from the age of four, closed out this world's teaching line, holding all of Scripture in memory instead of on a page.

documented_stories.teaser: Clement passes on a tradition about the apostle John, who rides out to bring back a young man turned robber chief. Clement calls it a true account handed down.
documented_stories.tellable_as: a story Clement told as true tradition about the Apostle John and a young man who fell
documented_stories.telling:
In a city not far from Ephesus, the aged apostle John once left a promising young man in the bishop's care. Clement, one of our teachers, passed this on as a true account, handed down and kept in memory.

The bishop taught the young man and baptized him. Then he relaxed his watch. The young man fell in with idle companions, and then with worse ones. At last he ran to the hills and became chief of a band of robbers.

Years later John came back and asked the bishop to return what he had left in his keeping. The bishop wept. The young man was dead to God, he said, a robber on the mountain. The old apostle tore his clothes, called for a horse and rode out to the mountain himself.

When the young man saw him, he fled. John forgot his age and rode after him. He begged his child not to run from his own father, old and unarmed. There was still hope of life for him, John said, and he would answer for him to Christ.

The young man stopped, threw down his weapons and wept. John led him back, prayed with him and fasted beside him in the struggle. He did not leave until he had restored him to the church.
documented_stories.title: The Apostle John and the Young Robber
documented_stories.when: Told by Clement, between about 180 and 215

documented_stories.teaser: Origen's father, Leonides, is arrested and held for beheading. His sixteen-year-old son wants to die beside him, and the boy's mother hides his clothes to keep him home.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the remembered account of how the persecution entered Origen's boyhood house
documented_stories.telling:
About the year 202, under the emperor Severus, persecution struck Alexandria. Leonides was arrested and held for beheading. His son Origen was sixteen. Eusebius tells what happened next in that house. He wrote a century later, from our church's memory, from Origen's own letters and from reports about him.

The boy burned to give himself up and die beside his father. His mother begged him to spare her, but he would not listen. So she hid all his clothes, and shame kept him at home.

Origen did the one thing left to him. He wrote to his father in prison. One line of that letter survives. "Take heed not to change your mind on our account."

Leonides did not change his mind. He was beheaded, and the family's property was seized. At seventeen, Origen was left the eldest of seven children, and his mother was a widow.
documented_stories.title: A Father in Prison and a Son Kept Home

documented_stories.teaser: Eusebius records a tradition about Potamiaena, a young woman put to death under Severus. It says she stood fast, and that the soldier who led her out later died a Christian.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The tradition of Potamiaena, a young woman put to death for her faith at Alexandria. This is how the church remembered her.
documented_stories.telling:
When Eusebius wrote, Potamiaena was still famous among the people of the country for all she had endured. Her story reached him already shaped by devotion.

She was a young woman put to death under the emperor Severus, and her mother Marcella died with her. She was threatened with what ancient cruelty kept for women, and she stood fast. The tradition says the judge sentenced her to die by burning pitch, poured slowly.

A soldier named Basilides led her out. The tradition says he held back the crowd's abuse with such gentleness that she told him to take courage. She promised, it says, to ask her Lord for him when she was gone.

Not long after, his fellow soldiers asked Basilides to swear an oath. He refused, because he was a Christian. At first they thought he was joking, but he was not. The tradition says he told them the reason. Potamiaena had come to him in the night and set a crown on his head.

Our church baptized him in prison. Then he was beheaded.
documented_stories.title: Potamiaena, as the Church Remembered Her
documented_stories.when: Under the emperor Severus, between 203 and 211

documented_stories.teaser: Eusebius reports that young Origen took a hard verse in Matthew at its word. His bishop first praised him and later denounced him, and some scholars doubt the act happened.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The remembered account, as Eusebius tells it, of a hard verse that Origen took at its word and acted on. Later his own bishop turned it against him. Some scholars doubt the act ever happened.
documented_stories.telling:
Origen was still young, and teaching the faith in Alexandria. He taught men and women together, day and night.

Eusebius alone tells what Origen did then, and no account from Origen himself describes it. Eusebius says Origen wanted no one to accuse him of wrong, so he took a hard verse from Matthew in the most literal sense. It speaks of those who "have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake." By this account he acted on it himself, and tried to keep it secret, but he could not. Eusebius calls the act immature, and in the same breath a proof of unusual faith.

When his bishop, Demetrius, learned of it, he admired the young man's daring and faith, and urged him to keep teaching. Later, once Origen had grown famous beyond Alexandria, the same Demetrius turned that youthful act against him. He wrote to bishops everywhere calling it foolish. He also attacked Origen's ordination by the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem.

Some later scholars thought the story came from misreading Origen's own figures of speech. Eusebius's English translator saw no reason to doubt it.

Origen himself later judged the verse differently. He wrote against reading it so literally.
documented_stories.title: A Hard Verse and a Young Teacher, as Eusebius Tells It
documented_stories.when: Origen's early teaching years; used against him in 231 or 232

documented_stories.teaser: Origen is ordained away from home, and his own bishop has not agreed to it. The bishop condemns it, and Origen never teaches in his city again.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the remembered rupture between the city's greatest teacher and its bishop
documented_stories.telling:
For years the teacher and the bishop held together. Demetrius governed our church and Origen taught, and the fame of the school filled the city.

Nearly all we know of what came next comes from Eusebius. He admired Origen, and he was hostile to the memory of Demetrius.

The break came over authority. On a journey through Palestine, Origen was ordained a presbyter by the bishops there. His own bishop had not agreed to it. Demetrius condemned the ordination, and the teacher with it.

Around his forty-sixth year, Origen left Alexandria for Caesarea. He never taught in the city again.
documented_stories.title: The Break Between Origen and His Bishop

documented_stories.teaser: At Caesarea, a student named Gregory thanks Origen in a farewell speech. He says the teaching came in stages, and that it kindled his love for the Word.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The student Gregory's own account of how Origen taught him. He gave it at his farewell.
documented_stories.telling:
Origen did not begin with doctrines, Gregory says. He began like a farmer testing soil. He questioned young Gregory and dug into his mind to see what it did under pressure.

Gregory had come from Neo-Caesarea, in Pontus, to study law. At Caesarea he met Origen, and he stayed some five years. He tells how he was taught in a farewell speech of praise, though some scholars have questioned who gave it, and when.

Logic came first, to make thinking honest. Next came the natural world, geometry and the stars, until the students' sense of wonder was trained. Then came ethics, formed as habits, with the teacher's own life teaching as well. Only then came theology. They read everything the philosophers and poets had said of God, with Scripture at the center.

Under all of it, Gregory says, something else was happening. Love was kindled in his inmost soul, like a spark falling there. It was love for the holy Word, and for this man who was the Word's friend. Gregory gave up the law. When at last he had to leave, he called it being driven out of paradise.
documented_stories.title: A Student's Farewell to Origen

documented_stories.teaser: In the Arsinoite district, villages follow the book of their late bishop Nepos. Dionysius comes out and sits with them for three days, going through it argument by argument.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Bishop Dionysius's own account of three days spent with the village churches near Arsinoe
documented_stories.telling:
The village churches near Arsinoe loved a bishop named Nepos. He had written a book against the allegorists. The promises in Scripture, he said, meant a thousand-year kingdom of plenty on this earth, plainly read. Nepos had died, and his book now ruled whole congregations. That book is lost. We know it only from the bishop who answered it.

Our bishop Dionysius went out to the villages. He told the story himself, in his book On the Promises, and Eusebius later quoted it. He called together the elders and the teachers, and any of the people who wished to come. For three days, from morning to evening, he sat with them and examined the book, argument by argument.

He wrote afterward that he loved Nepos for his faith, his hard work in the Scriptures and his psalms. Even so, he wrote, "the truth should be loved and honored most of all." He rejoiced in the constancy and sincerity of the believers, and in their willingness to reconsider as they weighed the arguments together.

At the end, Coracion, the leader of the other side, was persuaded. He said so in front of everyone. Some of the other believers, the account says, were glad at the spirit of agreement all had shown.
documented_stories.title: Three Days of Argument in the Villages
documented_stories.when: In the years Dionysius was bishop, about 248 to 264

documented_stories.teaser: Bishop Dionysius writes to the churches that most of his people did not run from the plague. They visited the sick and tended them, and many caught the sickness and died.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A true account from Bishop Dionysius's own letter. He wrote it while the plague was still raging.
documented_stories.telling:
A great sickness came to Alexandria about the year 260, and every house had its dead. Our bishop Dionysius wrote to the churches at festival time, while the plague still raged.

Most of the brothers and sisters did not run, he wrote. They visited the sick without fear, tended them day after day and served them in Christ.

Many caught the sickness from those they nursed, and they died of it. He wrote that they died most joyfully, as if drawing their neighbors' pain onto themselves. Our church buried its dead with open hands.

In the same letter, he said the pagans thrust away their own sick at the first sign of illness, and fled even from their dearest.
documented_stories.title: Nursing the Sick in the Plague

documented_stories.teaser: Palladius visits Didymus four times over ten years. The old teacher has been blind since the age of four, too young to have learned letters.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Palladius's own account of meeting Didymus, the blind author of Alexandria
documented_stories.telling:
Didymus lost his sight at four, he told Palladius, too young ever to have learned to read. Palladius met him four times over ten years and wrote down what he saw.

By then Didymus was old. What others took in with their eyes, he had taken in through his ears and held on to. He interpreted Scripture word by word. Palladius calls him the blind author.

Later tradition called him the seer, a name set against his blindness. Most of the books he wrote are lost to us, and only fragments were recovered, centuries later.

He died at the age of eighty-five.
documented_stories.title: The Blind Teacher Palladius Met

floor_note.text: This world held the same faith the Nicene council later put into words. Jesus is God's own Word, truly God, not merely like him. But one of its own greatest teachers held things more loosely. Origen speculated boldly toward ideas later councils rejected. He wondered whether souls existed before birth. He wondered whether all things would finally be restored. His own bishop condemned an irregular ordination, not these ideas. The dispute over the ideas themselves broke into open argument only at the very edge of this world's own record, decades after Origen died. A church council did not formally judge them until three centuries after that.

highlights.note: A port city in Egypt's Nile Delta, founded by Alexander the Great in 332 or 331 BCE. Its modern name is Iskandariya. This tradition grew in and around it.
A city on the coast of Roman Palestine. Its site, Qesaria, is in today's Israel. Origen lived and taught here.
Arsinoe was the capital of this district, called a nome. The city's site is Medinet el-Fayum, in today's Egypt. The villages that followed Nepos were here.
A Greek city of northwestern Anatolia, now İznik in Turkey. The council of 325 met here.

highlights.label: Council of Nicaea
highlights.note: A meeting of bishops in 325. It answered the teaching of Arius with the word homoousios.
The first teacher in this tradition whose name was kept. He taught about 180 to 200.
Clement was born about 150 and died about 215. He taught in the city from about 180. He left when persecution came under Severus.
Origen lived from about 185 to about 253. He taught in Alexandria until he broke with his bishop, then in Caesarea. Much of the writing that survives from this tradition is his.
He was bishop of Alexandria for forty-three years, until about 232.
Bishop of Alexandria from about 248 to 264. Before that he led the teaching. He led the church through persecution and plague.
An Egyptian bishop who wrote a book against the allegorists. He read the promises in Scripture as a thousand-year kingdom on earth.
He taught that the Son was the highest creature. The dispute over his teaching ran from about 318 to 381.
Born about 296, he was bishop of Alexandria from 328 to 373 and was exiled five times. His book On the Incarnation contains the line about people sharing God's life.

Didymus the Blind, about 309 or 313 to about 398. He took in Scripture through hearing and memory. Later tradition says he headed the school, though Palladius, Jerome and Socrates, who describe him, do not.

Eusebius of Caesarea, about 260 to 339, wrote a Church History. It is the main source for the line of teachers and for Origen's break with Demetrius. He is more reliable where he quotes documents than where he tells of succession.
Palladius of Galatia, about 363 to about 430. He wrote the Lausiac History in 419 and 420. It tells of his visits to Didymus.
A young woman put to death under Severus. Her story comes to us as a tradition that devotion has shaped.

highlights.label: Gregory of Neocaesarea
highlights.note: About 213 to about 270. He studied under Origen at Caesarea from about 233 to 238. The date and author of his farewell speech have been questioned.
Greek for the Word. It names God's own reason and speech, through whom all things were made and who became flesh in Jesus.
Reading Scripture at more than one level. There is a plain sense, and deeper senses about Christ and the soul. Egyptian Christians disagreed about it.
Greek for of one substance. The council at Nicaea used it to say the Son is fully God. Critics said the word is not in Scripture.
The thanksgiving meal of bread and cup at the center of worship. Members shared it whether or not they could read.
The statement of faith from the council at Nicaea in 325. It says the Son is of one substance with the Father.
The persecution of 249 to 251 bears his name. Origen was jailed and tortured in it.
A Roman emperor. In his reign, about 202, the hunt for Christians struck Alexandria, and Origen's father was put to death.
The soldier who led Potamiaena to her death. Eusebius counts him among Origen's disciples who died for the faith.
An office in the church. Clement taught that a good life came first, and the office came after it.
A great city of Ionia, in Asia Minor. Its ruins lie by Selçuk, in today's Turkey. Clement's story of John is set in a city near it.
Gregory's home city, in Pontus. Its site is Niksar, in today's Turkey.

legacy.text: Two things carried past this world's own horizon, in different ways. The first was a settled inheritance. This world passed on the Nicene confession, the hope of sharing God's own life, and Scripture read for a deeper meaning beneath its surface. Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus, teachers of a later generation, gathered an anthology of Origen's own writing while this world's own record was still open. The second thing was a live argument, not a settled one. Origen's boldest ideas kept being read, loved, and contested by turns. Interested translators carried them on both sides. The argument finally broke into open controversy right at this world's own edge.

read_first.note: Clement's flagship work for cultivated Greek readers - though its third book, on marriage and the body, survives in this edition only in Latin, not English.

source.citation: Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis (Miscellanies), trans. William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885)

read_first.note: Origen's boldest speculative work, reaching us only through Rufinus's own softened Latin translation - read alongside the Greek-derived Philocalia where the two overlap.

source.citation: Origen, De Principiis (On First Principles), trans. Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885)

read_first.note: The backbone story for this world's own people and events. Written a century later from Caesarea, with its own agenda. It is strongest where it quotes real documents, and weakest on tidy lists of who held office when.

source.citation: Eusebius of Caesarea, Historia Ecclesiastica (Church History), trans. Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers ser. 2 vol. 1 (1890)

relations_summary.text: This world's own relationship to the desert monks who came after it is real, but not settled. Real transmission toward the desert is well attested: a shared vocabulary of contemplation and ascent. One stronger claim is not established: that the desert's own way of life simply continues Alexandria's own formation logic. That claim is disputed. This world's own record does not resolve it alone.

sourcing.text: This world's record is richest in teaching and argument: the works of Clement, Origen, and Athanasius above all. It thins in a few important places. Clement's fullest treatment of marriage survives only in his own Greek; no public-domain English version has ever been made of it. Whether Alexandria's teaching tradition was one continuous, official school is itself live scholarly dispute, not something that can simply be reported as settled fact. And no woman's own words survive anywhere in this world's corpus.

story.text: From about 150 to 400 CE, Christians in Alexandria and across Egypt passed on one faith in two ways. Through long study together, teachers formed the few who could read. Baptism, the Eucharist and the yearly round of fasts and feasts reached everyone else.

Both ways answered to one center, the Logos. He is God's Word, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. Through him, Scripture, learning, worship and the remaking of a person became one movement toward one God.

Origen taught that Scripture, like a person, has body, soul and spirit. It has a plain sense and deeper senses that point to Christ and the soul. This way of reading is called allegoria. But the bishop Nepos wrote a book against it, and village churches in the Arsinoite district followed his book. After Nepos died, Bishop Dionysius answered them with three days of open argument, and the leader of the other side was persuaded.

Alexandria had a long tradition of Christian teachers and their pupils. The first name kept is Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher who became a Christian. Clement taught in the city from about 180. He praised his last teacher as the true bee. That teacher gathered from the flowers of the prophets and apostles, and left a deathless knowledge in his hearers' souls. Clement gives no name, and Eusebius says it was Pantaenus. Origen came after Clement, and Eusebius says he led the teaching of those preparing for baptism from his eighteenth year. Scholars disagree on whether a formal school stood behind these names before Origen's time.

A teacher and a bishop each held real authority, and the two never became one. The teacher's standing came from the wisdom people saw in him. The bishop held an office handed down. In the early 230s, Eusebius tells us, bishops in Palestine ordained Origen, the city's greatest teacher. His own bishop, Demetrius, had not agreed. He condemned the ordination and the teacher with it. Origen left for Caesarea and never taught in the city again.

Persecution came more than once. Origen's father was beheaded about 202. Origen himself was jailed and tortured under Decius. The church held two pictures of a life fully formed. One was the martyr's witness unto death. The other was the soul's long climb toward God. About 260, plague struck Alexandria. Bishop Dionysius wrote that most of his people did not run. They nursed the sick, and many caught the sickness and died.

Then the danger came from inside, as brothers argued over the very confession of the Word. Arius taught that the Son was the highest creature and not fully God. In 325 the council at Nicaea answered with the word homoousios, meaning of one substance with the Father. Athanasius, bishop from 328 to 373, defended it through five exiles. Later he wrote that the bishops had added nothing new. They had fenced what the churches had received. He also wrote that the Word became human so that people could share God's own life.

After Nicaea, the bishop of Alexandria became the guard of the creed across Egypt. His tools were letters, councils and exile. Among those who could read, the long bond between teacher and student was no longer the main way formation worked.

Later tradition ends the line of teachers with Didymus and says he headed the school in its last years. Didymus was blind from the age of four, too young to have learned letters. He died about 398, at eighty-five.

The Nicene creed and the hope of sharing God's life reached Eastern Christianity. So did the habit of reading Scripture with Christ at its center. Origen's work was carried forward too, and people loved it and argued over it.

dates.died: c. 253/4, Tyre, after imprisonment and torture under Decius: 'At this time Origen died, being sixty-nine years of age' (Eusebius)
dates.floruit: head of catechetical instruction from his eighteenth year (Eusebius); Alexandria until the Demetrius rupture c. 231-234, then Caesarea

voices.hedge: Origen's own surviving writing is a huge share of everything this world left behind. So the risk of mistaking his voice for the whole world's voice is real, and constant. Much of what he wrote survives only through translators with their own agenda. One, Rufinus, softened suspect passages. Another, Jerome, later quoted him unfavorably. Inside this world's own span, Origen was inherited and argued over, never condemned. A church condemned some of his ideas three centuries after this world's own record ends.
voices.text: Origen was this world's greatest and most contested teacher. He took over the school as a very young man, after his own father was martyred. As a youth he acted on a hard verse from Matthew far too literally, and his bishop, Demetrius, first admired him for it, then later used the same act against him. Origen wrote commentaries across almost all of Scripture, argued at length with pagan critics, and was finally imprisoned and tortured under the emperor Decius. He died of it a few years later.

dates.died: 373 (widely accepted). Socrates writes that he died 'in the second consulate of Gratian and Probus... having governed that church amidst the greatest perils forty-six years'. One modern editor reads that consulate as 371, and Jerome's Chronicle differs too. The difference is stated here, not settled.
dates.floruit: bishop 328-373, exiled five times; the dominant late-horizon voice

voices.hedge: Athanasius writes as a bishop in the middle of a fight. He is not a neutral historian. His decades of conflict can make doctrine look like this whole world's center, when it was really the loudest part of a longer, quieter story of teaching and worship. And Antony himself belongs at least as much to a different, later-forming world as to this one. Athanasius's own portrait is Alexandria's use of him, not the desert's own self-understanding.
voices.text: Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria for forty-six years, through five separate exiles. He defended one confession under real threat: the Son is truly God, of one substance with the Father. Arius had called the Son merely the highest creature. Near the end of this world's story, Athanasius put the hope of that confession into one line: God became human so that humans could share God's own life. He also wrote the best-known portrait of Antony, the desert's founding figure, holding him up as this city's own picture of a formed life.

dates.floruit: head of the teaching tradition, then bishop c. 248-264: the Decian persecution, the lapsed controversy, the plague, the Nepos affair

names.name: Dionysius of Alexandria ('the Great', bishop c. 248-264)

voices.hedge: Dionysius's own writings survive only as fragments. Later writers quoted him, kept what interested them, and let the rest go. His account of the three-day conference is his own telling of his own success. The side he argued against left no account of its own.
voices.text: Dionysius studied under Origen before becoming bishop himself. He led the church through two of this world's hardest tests: the Decian persecution and a citywide plague. He wrote that his own people nursed the dying without fear, while others in the city fled. When whole villages in the Egyptian countryside took up a teaching he thought was wrong, he did not condemn them from a distance. He traveled out, sat with them for three days, and won them back through patient argument.

dates.born: c. 309-313 (worked out from two ancient sources: Jerome, On Illustrious Men 109, written in 392/3, says he 'has already passed his eighty-third year', and Palladius, Lausiac History IV, gives 85 at his death)
dates.died: c. 398 (Palladius: 'He was 85 years old when he died')
dates.floruit: active as a teacher and biblical interpreter in Alexandria until his death in 398, remembered by later tradition as heading the catechetical school in its final line (not itself stated by the three loci cited here); blind from age four ('so he told me' - Palladius, eyewitness)

voices.hedge: No primary account actually calls Didymus the head of a school. That claim comes only from a later editor's own note, not an eyewitness. And almost none of his own books survive in a form anyone can read today. They were lost for over fifteen centuries, then found buried in the Egyptian sand. Their Greek has still not been translated into English.
voices.text: Didymus was blind from the age of four, too young to have ever read a written word himself. He held the whole of Scripture in memory, and taught from it for decades. Visitors came from far away to hear him. Later tradition remembers him as the last head of this world's teaching line, closing out its final generation.

tile.text: Between about 150 and 400 CE, Christians in Alexandria built a faith around teaching. Teachers led seekers through Scripture, layer by layer: the plain story first, then a deeper meaning underneath it, opening onto Christ himself. That reached the literate few. Ordinary believers met the same faith another way, through baptism, the shared meal, and the yearly round of fasts. Clement and Origen were confident that Greek learning could serve Christ, not threaten him. Two real authorities never merged here: the teacher's, earned by demonstrated wisdom, and the bishop's, handed down by office. When a young Origen took a hard verse from Matthew too literally and acted on it, his bishop first praised his zeal, then turned the same act against him years later. When plague struck the city, the bishop wrote that his own people nursed the dying while others fled. When villages came to disagree over how to read Scripture, another bishop sat with them for three days until they agreed. This world's own record was kept almost entirely by literate men. No woman's own words survive.
